comments.text:
Love the model. It makes a lot of sense technically.

The big question for me is: what actually forces this to happen? Today, EHRs and provider orgs don’t seem strongly incentivized to externalize authorization or rely on third-party trust frameworks.

Do you think this only becomes real with federal certification requirements, or is there a path where the market drives it?

comments.text:
I ran this past an AI reviewer and it asked: "which spec are you pointing to?" Of course my implicit but intentional answer is "none, yet." I guess I should explain.

Vendors, left to themselves, have little reason to build something that unbundles a function they currently control. That's not an indictment; it's just how market positions work. No one rushes to commoditize their own gate. And so the demand signal that would normally pull a standard into existence never forms.

A functional certification requirement changes that equation. It creates the incentive that the market on its own won't. Customers get a clear thing to expect, vendors get a clear reason to build it (and build it together, by collaborating on an open spec).

Am I thinking about SMART Permission Tickets? Sure, I hope that will be one possibility. But picking a technology today isn't the point. The goal here is to define the problem space and get the community exploring solutions together.

Jonas C. Sure, but are the largest EMRs going to do this "willingly" without the govt carrot & stick?   Are we still in extreme EMR data silos today without the existing govt certification requirements?

It would be ideal if billion dollar EMR corps would just have their data "open" and freely flowing on their own accord, but we know that isn't the way it usually works... data is literally monetized as much as possible, whenever possible.
